blocks.text: Coulomb's law is a fundamental principle in electrostatics that quantifies the force between two charged objects. The first measurement of the force between electric charges was made by the French physicist Charles de Coulomb. Coulomb's law is essential in understanding the behaviour of charged particles and the interactions that govern many electrical phenomena. On the basis of these measurements he deduced a law known as Coulomb's law.

blocks.title: Coulomb's law
blocks.text: The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F is proportional to q1 q2 / r^2, or F = k q1 q2 / r^2 ... (9.1).

Here F is the magnitude of the mutual force that acts on each of the two point charges q1 and q2, and r is the distance between them. The force F always acts along the line joining the two point charges (Fig. 9.1): like charges repel and unlike charges attract. k is the constant of proportionality; its value depends upon the nature of the medium between the two charges and the system of units in which F, q and r are measured. If the medium between the two point charges is free space and the system of units is SI, then k = 1/(4 pi eps0) ... (9.2), where eps0 is an electrical constant known as the permittivity of free space; in SI units its value is 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2. Substituting the value of eps0, k = 1/(4 pi eps0) = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2. Thus Coulomb's force in free space is F = (1/(4 pi eps0)) q1 q2 / r^2 ... (9.3).

If q1 exerts a force on q2, then q2 also exerts an equal and opposite force on q1. If we denote the force exerted on q2 by q1 as F21 and that on q1 due to q2 as F12, then F12 = -F21 ... (9.4). The magnitude of both forces is the same and is given by Eq. 9.3. To represent the direction of these forces we introduce unit vectors: if r21 (hat) is the unit vector directed from q1 to q2 and r12 (hat) is the unit vector directed from q2 to q1, then F21 = (1/(4 pi eps0)) (q1 q2 / r^2) r21 (hat) ... (9.5) and F12 = (1/(4 pi eps0)) (q1 q2 / r^2) r12 (hat) ... (9.6) (Fig. 9.2). Since r21 (hat) = -r12 (hat), these equations show that F21 = -F12. The signs of the charges determine whether the forces are attractive or repulsive.

If the medium between the two charges is an insulator, it is usually referred to as a dielectric. The presence of a dielectric always reduces the electrostatic force, compared with that in free space, by a certain factor which is a constant for the given dielectric. This constant is known as the relative permittivity and is represented by eps_r. Thus the Coulomb's force in a medium of relative permittivity eps_r is F = (1/(4 pi eps0 eps_r)) q1 q2 / r^2 ... (9.7). For air eps_r is 1.0006, which is so close to one that, with negligible error, Eq. 9.3 gives the electric force in air.

blocks.long_description: Two point charges push each other apart if they are alike and pull together if they are opposite, with a force along the line joining them that is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. In Example 9.1 the forces of two negative charges on a positive charge are added by components to give one resultant force. The field at a point is the force on a unit positive charge there. Field lines leave positive charges and end on negative ones; they are crowded where the field is strong, never cross, bend away from each other between like charges leaving a neutral point, and are parallel and evenly spaced between charged plates, where the field is uniform.

blocks.title: Example 9.1
blocks.text: Three point charges q1 = +40 uC, q2 = -60 uC and q3 = -50 uC lie in a plane: q2 is 0.15 m from q1, and q3 is 0.12 m from q1 along a line at 60 degrees to q1q2 (Fig. 9.2a). Find the net force on q1. Solution: F12 = k q1 q2 / r^2 = (9 x 10^9)(40 x 10^-6)(60 x 10^-6)/(0.15)^2 = 960 N, attractive, along q1q2. F13 = (9 x 10^9)(40 x 10^-6)(50 x 10^-6)/(0.12)^2 = 1250 N, attractive, at 60 degrees. Components: F13x = 1250 cos 60 = 625 N, F13y = 1250 sin 60 = 1075 N. Fx = 960 + 625 = 1585 N, Fy = 1075 N. F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2) = 1915 N. tan theta = 1075/1585 = 0.68, theta = 34 degrees with the line joining q1 and q2.

A Van de Graaff generator is an electrostatic generator which uses a moving belt to accumulate electric charge on a hollow metal globe on top of an insulated column, creating very high voltage direct current at low current levels. It was invented by the American physicist Robert J. Van de Graaff in 1929. Modern Van de Graaff generators can reach 5 megavolts, and a tabletop version can produce about 100 000 volts with enough energy to produce a visible spark. A pulley drives an insulating belt past a sharply pointed metal comb which has been given a positive charge by a power supply; electrons are removed from the belt, leaving it positively charged, and a similar comb at the top allows the net positive charge to spread to the dome (Do You Know).
